messages.author: 99bbda3b639a95c5
messages.subject: Single visit, multiple time intervals
parts:
Hello,

I am working with some unique data, and I have not found a post in this group about how to deal with it. I am using Breeding Bird Atlas data, where each site was only visited once (ever), and for each visit, bird observations were dividing into five 75-s time intervals. Here is a short version of what the data looks like:

Site     Species       T1  T2  T3  T4  T5  Time  Date  
1          NOBO         1    1    0    0    1     7:58   6-2
2          NOBO         0    0    1    0    0     7:02   6-8
2          NOBO         1    0    1    1    0     7:02   6-8
3          NOBO         0    0    0    0    1     8:35   6-9

As you can see, the challenge I'm encountering is how to deal with sites that had multiple birds detected. For sites with multiple birds, the birds often vary with regards to which time interval they were detected during. In total, there were 187 unique sites visited, but a total of 233 NOBOs recorded. I am ultimately interested in the site covs that influence occupancy, but I need to account for the observation covs. I have been creating models using the occu function, and believe that I could naively ignore any variables related to detection, in which case I could just use one of the birds per site (since the site covs would be the same). Alternatively, I have tried accounting for imperfect detection by considering each observation a "site" (i.e. 233 sites, one for each bird with site/obs covs duplicated for sites with multiple birds), but this does not seem to be a proper way to do so. The results change quite a bit depending on whether I use one bird per site (187 rows) or all birds, each considered as belonging to their own site (233 rows).

Thank you for your help, and any advice that can be provided on how I should work with this data would be much appreciated!

Best,
Connor

messages.author: d3fd439c2e48caf1
messages.subject: Re: Single visit, multiple time intervals
parts:
From your small snippet of data, it looks like a detection (or non-detection; i.e. 0 or 1) is recorded in each site in each of the five intervals. This may be obvious to others, but I'm unclear how you know that multiple birds were detected in different sites (you note 233 NOBOs recorded in total). Do you have other data (e.g., from trapping) that gives you information on individuals and their numbers per site? I'm also generally confused by what appears to be at least one detection (of one or more birds) in every site. Not much use in modeling occupancy if every site is known to be occupied ;).

Regarding one of your other questions (and generally speaking), you can (as you note) simply model detection as a constant (without covariates), or use interval number (1-5) as a continuous or categorical predictor of detection.

-Giancarlo

parts:
Hi Giancarlo,

Thanks for your response and comments. I did erroneously forget to mention that we have ~800 sites where there were no NOBO detections. If I'm understanding your question about multiple birds at a point, at a site such as site 2 in my example, those birds were two unique birds that were both vocalizing (e.g. one bird from the east, one bird from the west, allowing for a clear determination that there were in fact two birds). If I'm still not addressing your question please do let me know.

Thanks for your thoughts!

Connor

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Single visit, multiple time intervals
parts:
Dear Connor,

 you have encounter history data on individuals. If you aggregate those to site, producing frequencies of each unique encounter history, then you can fit the multinomial N-mixture models described in Chapter 7 of the AHM book. There is an example precisely like yours.  See page 351.

regards,
andy

Hi Andy,

Thank you for pointing me in the correct direction. That was exactly what I was looking for and was very helpful to me.

One final question: I noticed that the resulting predictions for each site are abundance, rather than occupancy. I am interested in simply predicting occupancy, as the majority of my count data are 1s, with very few sites having 2s and 3s. How can I get the predicted occupancy probability? I found the formula psi = 1 - exp(-lambda) in a previous thread; would this be the correct equation to use here to convert?

Best,
Connor
